¶
'''tosca''' (tos′kä), ''n.'' [< Sp. Pg. ''tosco'' (fem. ''tosca''), rough, coarse.] A name given in parts of South America, especially near the mouth of the La Plȧta river, and in the region of the pampas generally, to a soft concretionary limestone, having about the consistence of slightly baked clay, and of a dark-brown color. {{smaller|It underlies the so-called Pampean formation. The name ''tosca'' is said also to be applied in parts of southern Italy, and especially in Sicily, to varieties of pumiceous tuffs. In the gold-mining regions of the United States of Colombia the word ''tosca'' is also in frequent use as designating a very peculiar rock lying near the surface, and said by some to be of volcanic origin, but not yet scientifically described. It differs very much from the tosca of the Pampean region.}}

'''toscatter†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''toscateren''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''scatter''.] To scatter in pieces.

{{smaller block|Lo, ech thyng that is oned in it selve
Is more strong than whan it is ''toscatered''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Summoner's Tale, l. 261.}}}}

'''tose''' (tōz), ''v. t.'' [Also ''toze'', formerly also ''toaze''; < ME. ''tosen'' (< AS. *''tāsan''), a common form of ''tesen'', whence mod. E. ''tease'': see ''tease'', and cf. ''touse''.] 1. To pull about or asunder; touse.

{{smaller block|What shepe that is full of wulle
Upon his backe thei ''tose'' and pulle
Whyle ther is any thynge to pille.
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., Prol.}}}}

'''toshiver†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''toshiveren, toschiveren''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''shiver''<sup>1</sup>.] To break in pieces.
{{smaller block|The kniȝt spere in speldes al ''toschiuered.''
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3603.}}}}

'''toshnail''' (tosh′nāl), ''n.'' A nail driven in aslant, like a tosh. ''Halliwell.''

'''toshred†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''toshreden, toschreden''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''shred.''] To cut in shreds.
{{smaller block|The helmes they tohewen and ''toshrede.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight's Tale, l. 1751.}}}}

'''tosiness''' (tō′zi-nes), ''n.'' The state or property of being tosy. Also ''toziness.''
{{smaller block|''Tozyness'', Softness, like tozed Wooll. {{right|''Bailey'', 1727.}}}}

'''tosliter†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''toslyteren''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''sliteren'', freq. of ''sliten'', slit: see ''slit''<sup>1</sup>.] To make artificial slashes or openings in, as a dress.
{{smaller block|Wrought was his robe in straunge gise,
And al ''toslytered'' for queyntise,
In many a place, lowe and hie.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 840.}}}}

'''toslive†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''tosliven''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''slive''<sup>1</sup>.] To cleave or split in pieces.
{{smaller block|And laiden on with swerdes clere,
Helm and scheld that stronge were
Thai gonne hem al ''toschlive.''
{{right|''Gy of Warwike'', p. 471. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

'''tosliver†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''toslyveren''; < ''to-''<sup>2</sup> + ''sliver.''] To split into slivers or small pieces.
{{smaller block|The noyse of foulis for to ben delyvered
So loude rong, "Have don and lat us wende,"
That wel wende I the wode had al ''toslyvered'' [var. ''to-''

{{RunningHeader|tory|6397|toss}}{{smaller block|porters.{{right|''Lecky'', Eng. in 18th Cent., i.}}}} 4. [''cap.''] In ''American hist.'', a member of the British party during the Revolutionary period; a loyalist. {{smaller|The Tories were very numerous, especially in the Middle and Southern colonies, and many of them took arms for the king. They were frequently severely persecuted, and after the war many of them emigrated to Canada and elsewhere.}} {{smaller block|Washington will not trust us with the keeping of a suspected ''Tory'', if we let the rascal trifle in this manner with the corps.{{right|''J. F. Cooper'', The Spy, xxix.}}}} 5. [''cap.''] In general, a conservative; one who favors established authority and institutions, especially in a monarchy or an aristocracy; a person of aristocratic principles, as opposed to a democrat or a radical. {{smaller block|Purrus Ram and Khoom Dass are in attendance, and fear greatly that the party of the Viziers, to whom they are opposed, will hurl them from power, and that the ''Tories'' of Bussahir will triumph.{{right|''W. H. Russell'', Diary in India, II. 191.}}}} {{smaller block|'''High Tory''', an upholder or advocate of an extreme type of Toryism.}} '''II.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to or characteristic of tories, in any sense; specifically [''cap.''], belonging or relating to the Tories: as, a ''Tory'' government; ''Tory'' principles or measures. See I. {{smaller block|"Surrender! you servants of King George," shouted the leader, . . . "or I will let a little of your ''tory'' blood from your veins."{{right|''J. F. Cooper'', The Spy, xxii.}}}} {{smaller block|The party led by Sir Robert Peel no longer called itself "''Tory'','' but "Conservative." ''Contemporary Rev.'', LI. 4.}} {{smaller block|'''Tory Democracy''', the principles or views of the Tory Democrats; also, the Tory Democrats collectively.—'''Tory Democrats''', in ''recent British politics'', those members of}} the Conservative party who are supposed to incline more or less to democratic ideas and methods. ¶ '''toryism''' (tō′ri-izm), ''n.'' [< ''tory'' + ''-ism.''] The principles, methods, and practices of tories, in any sense; specifically [''cap.''], those of the British Tories. {{smaller block|Nothing would illustrate the subject better . . . than an inquiry into the rise and progress of our late parties, or a short history of ''toryism'' and whiggism from their cradle to their grave, with an introductory account of their genealogy and descent. {{right|''Bolingbroke'', Parties, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|The times have been dreadful, and old families like to keep their old tenants. But I dare say that is ''Toryism.'' {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, viii.}}}} '''Toryminæ''' (tor-i-mī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Torymus'' + ''-inæ.''] A notable subfamily of parasitic hymenopterous insects, of the family ''Chalcididæ'', conspicuous from their brilliant metallic colors and their long ovipositor: originally named as a family ''Torymidæ'' by Watson in 1833. {{smaller|They are the commonest parasites of the cynipid and cecidomyidan gall-makers, although some have been reared from the cells of burrowing bees and a few from lepidopterous larvæ. About 200 species are known.}} '''Torymus''' (tor′i-mus), ''n.'' [NL. (Dalman, 1820).] A genus of hymenopterous parasites of gall-making insects, typical of the subfamily ''Toryminæ.'' '''tory-rory†''' (tō′ri-rō′ri), ''a.'' [Appar. a varied redupl. of ''tory.''] Wild; boisterous; harum-scarum. {{smaller block|Lift up your voices, and sing like nightingales, you ''tory rory'' jades. Courage, I say; as long as the merry pence hold out, you shall none of you die in Shoreditch. {{right|''Dryden'', Kind Keeper, iv. 1.}}}} '''tosca''' (tos′kä), ''n.'' [< Sp. Pg. ''tosco'' (fem. The name ''tosca'' is said also to be applied in parts of southern Italy, and especially in Sicily, to varieties of pumiceous tuffs. In the gold-mining regions of the United States of Colombia the word ''tosca'' is also in frequent use as designating a very peculiar rock lying near the surface, and said by some to be of volcanic origin, but not yet scientifically described. It differs very much from the tosca of the Pampean region.}} '''toscatter†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. [Also ''tozer''; < ''tose'' + ''-er''1.] One who toses; specifically, a teaser of wool. ''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXXV. 812. [Prov. Eng.] '''tosh'''1 (tosh), ''a.'' [Said to be < OF. ''tousé'', ''touzé'', clipped, shorn, pared round, < L. ''tondere'', pp. ''tonsus'', clip, shear: see ''tonsure''.] Neat; trim. [Scotch.] {{smaller block|The hedges will do; I clipped them wi' my ain hand last back-end; and, nae doubt, they make the avenue look a hantle ''tosher''. {{right|''Wilson'', Margaret Lindsay, p. 271.}}}} '''tosh'''2 (tosh), ''n.'' A variant of ''tush''1. ''Halliwell.'' '''toshach''', ''n.'' See ''toisech''. '''toshake†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''toshaken''; < AS. ''tōsceacan'', shake to pieces, < ''tō-'', apart, + ''sceacan'', shake: see ''to-''2 and ''shake''.] To shake violently; shake to pieces. {{smaller block|Glad was he to londe for to hye,
So was he with the tempest al ''toshake''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 962.}}}} '''toshear†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''tosheren''; < AS. ''tōsceran'', cut apart, < ''tō-'', apart, + ''sceran'', shear: see ''to-''2 and ''shear''1.] To cut in two. {{smaller block|The God of love . . . al ''toshare''
Myn herte with his arwis kene. {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 1858.}}}} '''toshend†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''toshenden''; < ''to-''2 + ''shend''.] To ruin utterly; destroy. {{smaller block|I had been deed and al ''toshent''
But for the precious oynement. {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 1903.}}}} '''toshiver†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''toslyteren''; < ''to-''2 + ''sliteren'', freq. of ''sliten'', slit: see ''slit''1.] To make artificial slashes or openings in, as a dress. {{smaller block|Wrought was his robe in straunge gise, And al ''toslytered'' for queyntise, In many a place, lowe and hie. {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 840.}}}} '''toslive†''', ''v. t.'' [ME. ''tosliven''; < ''to-''2 + ''slive''1.] To cleave or split in pieces. {{smaller block|And laiden on with swerdes clere, Helm and scheld that stronge were Thai gonne hem al ''toschlive.'' {{right|''Gy of Warwike'', p. 471. (''Halliwell.'')}}}} '''tosliver†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. ''toslyveren''; < ''to-''2 + ''sliver.''] To split into slivers or small pieces. {{smaller block|The noyse of foulis for to ben delyvered So loude rong, "Have don and lat us wende," That wel wende I the wode had al ''toslyvered'' [var. ''to''{{smaller block|''shivered''].{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 493.}}}} '''toss''' (tos), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''tossed'' or ''tost'', ppr. ''tossing''. [Early mod. E. ''tosse''; < late ME. ''tossen''; origin unknown: (''a'') prob. < Norse ''tossa'', strew, scatter; (''b'') otherwise < D. ''tassen'', < F. ''tasser'', heap up, as the waves of a troubled sea (< ''tas'', a heap (see ''tass''1); for the variation of form, cf. ''tassel''1, ''tossel''1). The W. ''tosio'', jerk, toss (< ''tos'', a quick jerk, a toss), is not supported by cognate Celtic forms, and is prob. from E.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To lift, heave, or throw up with a sudden, impatient, or spirited movement; jerk: as, to ''toss'' one's head. {{smaller block|Som savage Bull . . . ''tosses'' his head on high, Wounds with his hooves the Earth, with horns the sky. {{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas's Battle of Ivry.}}}} {{smaller block|He ''tossed'' his arm aloft.{{right|''Addison'', Cato, iv. 4.}}}} '''2.''' To jerk or fling to and fro; heave or pitch up and down or from one place to another; tumble or throw about. {{smaller block|Howbeit the wroughte sees ''tossyd'' and rolled vs ryght greuously.{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 73.}}}} {{smaller block|That we henceforth be no more children, ''tossed'' to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine. {{right|Eph. iv. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|Islanders, whose bliss Is to be ''tossed'' about from wave to wave. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 300.}}}} '''3.''' In ''mining'', to separate (ore) from the gangue by stirring (tossing) the slimes with water in a keeve, and then allowing the heavier, one end resting on the ground, an operation which may be continued from a quarter of an hour to an hour. {{smaller|The packing facilitates the separation of the ore by the vibrating motion imparted to the particles. This process is generally done by hand, but sometimes by a mechanical arrangement. It was formerly somewhat extensively employed in the tin-mining districts of Cornwall, England, and has not entirely gone out of use.}} 4. To cast; pitch; fling; hurl; specifically, to throw with the palm of the hand upward; throw lightly or carelessly. {{smaller block|I ''tosse'' a balle. . . . I had as leve ''tosse'' a ball here alone as to play at the tenys over the corde with the. {{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 760.}} Choler adust congeals our blood with fear, Then black bulls ''toss'' us, and black devils tear. {{right|''Dryden'', Cock and Fox, l. 157.}} Like the old giants that were foes to Heaven They heave ye stool on stool and fling main pot-lids, Like massy rocks, dart ladles, ''tossing'' irons And tongs like thunderbolts. {{right|''Fletcher'', Woman's Prize, ii. 5.}} One person ''tosses'' the halfpenny up, and the other calls at pleasure head or tail. {{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 439.}}}} 5. Figuratively, to disquiet; agitate; set in commotion, as by shifting opinions, feelings, circumstances, or influences; disturb; disorder. {{smaller block|Was never Lady loved dearer day Then she did love the knight of the Redcrosse, For whose deare sake so many troubles her did ''tosse''. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. vii. 27.}} Madly ''toss'd'' between desire and dread. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 171.}} Calm region once, And full of peace, now ''tost'' and turbulent. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 1126.}}}} 6. To pass from one to another, as in conversation or discussion; bandy. {{smaller block|Is it such an Entertainment to see Religion worryed by Atheism, and Things the most Solemn and Significant tumbled and ''tost'' by Buffoons? {{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 138.}}}} {{smaller block|Then she, who . . . heard her name so ''tost'' about, Flush'd slightly at the slight disparagement. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}} '''7'''†. To turn over and over; busy one's self with; turn the leaves of, as a book or lesson. {{smaller block|I will to Athens, there to ''tosse'' my bookes. {{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 99.}}}} {{smaller block|''Tit.'' Lucius, what book is that she ''tosseth'' so? ''Young Luc.'' Grandsire, 'tis Ovid's Metamorphoses. . . . ''Tit.'' Soft! see how busily she turns the leaves! {{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iv. 1. 41.}}}} '''8.''' To toss up with. See ''to toss up'', under II. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|To ''toss'' the pieman is a favourite pastime with costermongers' boys and all that class. . . . If the pieman win the toss, he receives 1''d.'' without giving a pie; if he lose, he hands over a pie for nothing. {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 206.}}}} '''9.''' Same as ''to toss off'' (''a'') (which see, below). {{smaller block|I mean to ''toss'' a can, and remember my sweetheart, afore I turn in. ''Congreve'', Love for Love, iii. 15.}} '''10.''' To dress hastily or smartly; trick: with ''out''. [Rare.] {{smaller block|I remember, a few days ago, to have walked behind a damsel, ''tossed out'' in all the gaiety of fifteen; her dress was loose, unstudied, and seemed the result of conscious beauty.{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 2.}}}} '''To toss in a blanket''', to toss (a person) upward from a blanket held slackly at the corners and edges, and jerked vigorously up and down, the person tossed being sometimes thrown as high as the ceiling. This was formerly a favorite form of the expression of popular dislike. It is also practised in schools, among sailors, etc. Compare ''haze''2, ''v. t.'', 2, ''hazing.'' {{smaller block|A rascally slave! I will ''toss'' the rogue ''in a blanket.''{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 240.}}}} {{smaller block|I shall certainly give my solitary voice in favour of religious liberty, and shall probably be ''tossed in a blanket'' for my pains.{{right|''Sydney Smith'', To Lady Holland, Jan. 17, 1813.}}}} '''To toss off.''' (''a'') To take off; drink off, as a dram. {{smaller block|For in a brave vein they ''tost off'' the bouls.{{right|''Robin Hood and Maid Marian'' (Child's Ballads, V. 375).}}}} {{smaller block|The corporal produced the bottle and the glass, poured it out, made his military salute, and ''tossed'' it ''off.''{{right|''Marryat'', Snarleyyow, xxxii.}}}} (''b'') To dispose of; pass off; while away: said of time. {{smaller block|Have you read Cynthia? It is a delightful thing to ''toss off'' a dull hour with.{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, ii. 1.}}}} '''To toss the oars''' (''naut.''). See ''oar''1.—'''To toss up''', to prepare hastily, especially by cooking. {{smaller block|On Saturday stew'd beef, with something nice,
Provided quick, and ''toss'd up'' in a trice.{{right|''W. King'', The Vestry.}}}} {{smaller block|Amid these rich and potent devices of the culinary art . . . poor Hepzibah was seeking for some nimble little titbit, which, with what skill she had, and such materials as were at hand, she might ''toss up'' for breakfast.{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, vii.}}}}
